Tengo que reconocer que el western no es un género que me atraiga especialmente y que, en ocasiones, puede llegar a hacérseme algo repetitivo, pero tenía una deuda con esta película y muchas ganas de verla, y he de decir que me ha dejado una sensación completamente distinta. A pesar de sus casi tres horas, no he sentido que se me hiciera realmente pesada, y eso me parece uno de sus mayores méritos, si bien es cierto que hay algún momento en el que el ritmo se resiente y algunas partes se podrían haber acortado. Leone se toma su tiempo, pero sabe perfectamente cómo utilizarlo. Cada plano, cada silencio, cada mirada y cada duelo están construidos con una clara intencionalidad. La película tiene una personalidad enorme, unos paisajes espectaculares (joder, qué bonita es España), una fotografía increíble y una puesta en escena que hace que hasta los momentos más pausados tengan algo que decir. Los tres protagonistas funcionan y se complementan ciertamente bien, y me ha dejado especialmente buen sabor de boca que ninguno sea el típico héroe o villano perfectamente definido, sino que todos se muevan por sus propios intereses y tengan su propia moral. Además, la banda sonora es absolutamente brutal y consigue elevar muchas escenas que ya de por sí funcionan, especialmente en el tramo final, donde se respira pura tensión hasta el último segundo. Una película que entiendo perfectamente que sea considerada un clásico.

Una grandissima trilogia assolutamente da vedere

La musique est encore une sublime et culte. J’aime beaucoup la relation qui s’établit entre le bon et le truand qui se trahissent mutuellement jusqu’au dernier moment, ça change du précédent. Toutefois, l’ambiance guerre de sécession m’a moins accroché que le western pur et dur. J’ai trouvé également que le rythme du film est très irrégulier, ce qui est dommage pour un film de cette trempe. Heureusement que la scène finale vient sublimé tout ça, car on aurait presque oublié la brute tout du long du film

É curioso ver como os princípios dos Estados Unidos da América aparecem de maneira sutil, mas profundamente relevantes. Caso não sabermos desses tais princípios, o filme todo se torna sem sentido, o herói se torna sem sentido. O filme é uma melodia bélica. No fim, o que move o mundo é o dinheiro, ele compra armas, compra trabalho, compra a moral, compra a vida e compra a morte. Assim, o filme segue, os personagens sempre acossados pela guerra, mas o dinheiro é mais importante. Esse filme é o que mais evidencia isso, pois os antecessores tinham uma trama mais localizada e pessoal, esse filme não, ele possui uma guerra gigantesca que acompanha o filme todo. A cena final é um caso a parte, ela me parece até cômica, se não fosse séria, estamos vendo os três cowboys cercados por tumultos, onde todos estão preenchidos por mortos de guerra, mortos por armas de fogo, e o que os três fazem? Decidem o seu mérito em um duelo de pistolas - curioso, no mínimo.

This film is pretty much flawless. It's kind of baffling that Leone even bothered plagiarising Kurosawa when he had this kind of cinematography up his sleeve - the way its shot is incredibly tasteful and innovative. Obviously the soundtrack is great, and while the script is simple that makes it charming in its own right. The actors get the most they can out of it, and any lack of intrinsic emotion in the wordplay is made up for by the intensity of their expressions - there's a kind of glint in their eyes that gives an unmistakably fiery passion to every scene.

枪的战斗迅雷不及掩耳，而莱昂内成功利用电影语言延宕了枪与枪的对决。不发一言的角色，脸部特写的切换，时间酝酿了空间的紧张感，关注瞄准与被瞄准的辩证关系，耐心等待时机后才是期待已久的一枪毙命。莱昂内的音乐是不断重复的旋律动机，尴尬时刻所导致的窘迫感，抑或是成功突围陷阱的崛起，是全片反反复复的主题。幽默感的存在，又是对严肃西部电影的革新，这也是现代牛仔精神覆灭的体现，类似黑泽明眼中的日本武士精神，在现代性的浪潮下土崩瓦解。布遍粗粝的真实感，人物脸部的残痕类同砖瓦的破败，蚊子甚至还肆无忌惮地在演员脸上爬动，被摄影机一并捕获。三个家伙皆为利来，行动线因利益关系不断调整变化。财宝之路碰上国家士兵，两种战斗动机的比对。结尾三人大战是影史经典，不是演员的动作，而是摄影的动作，是剪辑的动作，是音乐的动作。

I couldn’t predict a single thing that happened in this movie. This movie was so filled with energy and life to the point where I couldn’t even fathom somebody writing the story, the  entirety of the story just felt so unscripted, so natural, so sudden that every scene I was wondering, what are the writers gonna do here? Where can they take it from here? And I never ever had a clear answer. With modern movies it feels like I always know what the writer is planning to do next, but throughout this entire movie, I was just constantly flabbergasted at the concept that somebody sat down and thought of the story and wrote it down. Something else I’d like to mention that I noticed in this movie that when comparing it to modern media struck me as so fresh and new with the amount of quiet waiting, there was in this movie. This movie is full of moments where the characters wait and listen and think, where the actors truly get to shine and let their expressions speak for themselves. Which not only added to the realism of it all, but also opened up opportunities for so much more storytelling storytelling that felt much more deep and grounded and real. It feels like in modern movies the directors expect the audience to be stupid, they say everything so unbelievably clear. There is nothing expected of you, everything is just laid out clearly, but in this movie, a lot of the movie is just facial expressions, eye movements, little subtle hints of story that you have to pick up on on your own and I love it.

Un western spaghetti ? C'est peu dire. Sergio Leone prend un malin plaisir à dynamiter le genre américain par excellence en créant une nouvelle mythologie autour de trois personnages inoubliables et aussitôt classiques. Blondin, le bon, l'est surtout pour sa gueule. Sentenza, la brute, l'est avec tous ceux qui se mettent sur son chemin. Tuco, le truand, n'est qu'une petite frappe sans envergure, mais plutôt attachante. Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef et Eli Wallach au sommet de leur art, lancés dans une incroyable chasse au trésor. Et en prime : la musique d'Ennio Morricone...

Laden with thematic depth and reflections on violence, relationships, money, and obviously the intersections of those three, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly may be a little too long but it’s also far more emotionally engaging than the other films in the Dollars trilogy. Eli Wallach’s scenes around the halfway mark, convincing himself and Blondie both that he truly cares for him are an incredible showcase of talent and bring the film’s ideas into focus. When Clint Eastwood shows up in the town to help Tuco shoot his way through Angel Eyes’s crew of bandits, asking him “Were you gonna die alone?” the bizarro brotherhood between these characters is crystal clear. They love each other, they have each other’s backs, but Tuco in particular can’t stop himself from stabbing Blondie in the back. Blondie knows this, and just accepts that that’s the way it is - he treats Tuco accordingly. From there we move to the bridge sequence, as pointed a war satire as there ever was, and finally, what is probably, for my money, the greatest sequence in movie history, the cemetery. With a bit more research and a couple of ancillary texts, I could probably write a few thousand words on the overwhelming scale of the setting and the goal of the characters in being there. My final (and initial) thoughts on this movie are that this is not Sergio Leone, Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef, or even Eli Wallach’s movie (although he has quite a claim to it). It’s Ennio Morricone’s. Every single scene is not just elevated by the music, it’s made by it. This score is so perfect, so tonally dialed-in, that it carries the movie even more than John Williams’s work on The Empire Strikes Back does. Of course, in the case of Star Wars , the music doesn’t need to support every scene in the same way. In a movie like this one, with sparse dialogue and beautiful yet largely unexciting visuals, the music is able to be the main character. It fits each scene like off-the-rack pants fit a 5’10”, 160lb white man - that is to say, nothing has ever fit better. It’s considered one of the best of all time for a reason, but it really does stand out as exceptional in an already incredible movie.

No need for me to go into deep detail to illustrate this film. Any cool things you saw in later Western films and games came from Sergio Leone's "Dollars" trilogy. Quentin Tarantino shamelessly ripped scenes off to make his own classics. I can't blame him; a great artist should know how to steal.  Leone invented a perfect formula for colorful, yet gritty period films. The Good, the Bad and the Ugly has it all: iconic characters, grand-scale journey, clever twists, cool gunslinging action, and off-the-charts badassery. Even "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" became a popular tagline. Ennio Morricone's legendary score remains the golden standard for the entire Western genre. Obvious audio dubbing is a "bad" part of the film, but it is also part of the old movie charm. In the early days of cinema, filmmakers worked around limitations to realize their vision. Sergio Leone and his crew built an epic cinematic monument that dwarfs most modern blockbusters.

The film begins by introducing its three main characters. And it does it so brilliantly that it might just have one of the greatest character introductions in cinema history. Clint Eastwood plays the Good — Blondie, as he is called in the film. Lee Van Cleef plays the Bad — Angel Eyes. And Eli Wallach plays the Ugly — Tuco. Although all three performances are excellent, Eli Wallach's performance as Tuco is easily my favorite. He gets more screen time than the other two, but more importantly, somehow manages to become incredibly likable despite being, well… Tuco. Coming from extreme poverty, Tuco has embraced banditry and has absolutely no idea what morality even means. He's selfish, greedy, opportunistic, and constantly looking for the easiest way to make money. Blondie, on the other hand, is a lone wolf who lives by his own rules. And then there's Angel Eyes — compared to the other two, he's more refined and knows exactly how to position himself alongside whoever holds the power. During the Civil War, for example, he rises to the rank of colonel and uses the army to further his own interests. In that sense, the three characters can almost be seen as three different social types: The Bad is disciplined, military, and part of the system. The Good is a scruffy outsider who refuses to belong to any system. The Ugly is essentially a poor man from the countryside who has chosen banditry and is desperately looking for a shortcut to wealth. And that's what makes the three characters so interesting: these aren't just Western archetypes. They're three types of people we can still recognize around us today.
